catalog_quote: Phonological words in Atong are stressed on their final syllable. Stress can be shifted to any other syllable for emphasis or contrastive purposes. I adopt the definition stated by Van Der Mark that phonetic stress is [...] Stress in Atong can be marked by all of these variables and consonant lengthening. In Atong vowel quality does not necessarily change in stressed or unstressed syllables. Only in unstressed syllables containing the vowel /ə/ can this vowel assimilate to the vowel in the next syllable. Extra high pitch or falsetto voice in Atong is always accompanied by extra lengthening of the vowel and is a phonetic means to mark greater intensity of the meaning of whatever morpheme is stressed. 2.3 CONSONANT LENGTH

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word carries one stress, on its last syllable (the 'variables' referred to are the phonetic correlates of stress quoted from Van Der Mark 2003: pitch, loudness, length; Atong adds consonant lengthening). Stress can be moved to any other syllable for emphasis or contrast, so it is not lexically contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any snippet examined; the 2019 text says a phonological word 'has one stressed syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is shiftable to any syllable for emphasis/contrast (2014: 37). The author later qualified the rule: Atong Texts (2019: 16-17): 'Although van Breugel (2014a: 37) claims that phonological words are stressed on their final syllable, this appears not always to be the case. Although it is mostly true for words and expressions in isolation, as when a native speaker teaches a visiting linguist a new word or expression, it is not always the case in normal, connected speech or discourse. In normal discourse, stress assignment seems highly variable. The same word can be stressed differently by the same speaker in different utterances. What determines stress assignment within the phonological word is not fully understood, and certainly merits further study.' The 2021 Dictionary (introduction) repeats: 'stress of this phonological word is usually on the last syllable, but can occur on any other syllable as well, for reasons not fully understood by the author.' Grammar also notes a word whose 'first syllable is stressed' in the consonant-length section (p. 39 area).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, which in Atong can span a quantified noun plus its quantifier phrase (Dictionary 2021) and runs to five or six syllables (Texts 2019). The final-stress rule holds most reliably for words and expressions elicited in isolation (citation forms); in connected speech stress placement is reported as variable.
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level aton1241 (ISO aot). All three sources are by the same fieldworker and describe Atong of the South Garo Hills (Meghalaya) and adjacent Bangladesh; no differently named variety or dialect split is at issue in the passages seen. The 2019 and 2021 works are the author's own later qualifications of the 2014 rule, not descriptions of a different variety.

readall_conflicts: The standing tension already held by the project remains between van Breugel 2014a: 37 ('Phonological words in Atong are stressed on their final syllable', shiftable for emphasis/contrast), which the catalog encodes as fixed: final syllable, and the same author's later hedges (2019: 16-17, final stress holds mostly for citation forms, 'In normal discourse, stress assignment seems highly variable'; 2021 dictionary intro, stress 'usually on the last syllable.. not fully understood by the author'). Those later statements qualify rather than replace the final-stress default.
